lessons.title: Man macht das so: holiday places and what you do there
lessons.goal: Say what people can do in a holiday place, using man with any verb and with modals, and name six holiday places.

grammar.point: man means people in general and always takes the er/sie verb form: man schwimmt, man kann schwimmen, man darf nicht campen.
grammar.oneLine: Am Meer kann man schwimmen. Was kann man hier machen?

mistake.why: man takes the er/sie form of the verb, so kann and not können.

terms.meaning: a little word for people in general: one, you, they
the verb form that goes with er and sie, like schwimmt or kann
a helper verb like kann, darf or muss
the modal in part 2 and the infinitive at the very end

cards.title: Before we start: a holiday, and what you can do there
cards.body: Chapter 12 is about holidays: what you do at the sea, what you pack, a city tour, a route, the weather and a postcard. Today you say what people can do in a holiday place. You know Hier darf man nicht rauchen from the rules lesson. Now you use man for holiday tips too.

examples.why: You know this already: man + darf + a verb at the end.

examples.en: At the sea you can swim.
examples.why: New today: the same man pattern for a holiday tip.

examples.en: In a café people drink coffee.
examples.why: New today: man with a normal verb, no modal. The verb after man ends in -t.

steps: You already know: Hier darf man nicht rauchen (chapter 8) and modals with a verb at the end (chapter 5)
New today: man for people in general, with the er/sie form, and six holiday places
By the end you can: say what people can do at the beach, the lake or in the forest, and ask Was kann man hier machen?
cards.more: Imagine a friend asks: What can you do on holiday? You do not talk about one person. You talk about everybody: people swim, people hike, people camp. German has a little word for that, man. You already met it on the sign Hier darf man nicht rauchen. Today you use it for fun things, not only for rules. First you meet six holiday places, then three new holiday verbs, then you build tips like Am See kann man baden.

cards.title: Holiday places: der Strand, das Meer, der Berg
cards.body: Six holiday places. To say where you are, learn the little pieces: am Strand, am Meer, am See, im Wald, auf einer Insel. Mountains are usually plural: in den Bergen. Learn each noun with its article and its plural.

examples.en: Mira is reading in the forest.

examples.de: Ben macht Urlaub auf einer Insel.
examples.en: Ben is on holiday on an island.
examples.why: auf einer Insel: on an island

cards.more: Think of six postcards. On each postcard there is one place. Under the picture you write the little piece you need: am Strand, am Meer, am See, im Wald, in den Bergen, auf einer Insel. You do not build these pieces yet. You just learn the whole piece with the noun, like a name tag. Example: you sit by the water of a lake, so you say am See. You walk between the trees, so you say im Wald.
cards.lead: After the intro, here are the six places. The little words am, im and in den answer Wo? (where?). You use them here as ready pieces with each noun, so you can say where you are.

deeper.text: Careful with See: der See is a lake, but die See is the sea. You meet die See in two big names in the north of Germany: die Nordsee and die Ostsee. So am See means at a lake, an der Ostsee means at the Baltic Sea. The plural die Seen always means lakes.

example.de: Im Sommer fahren wir an die Ostsee.
example.en: In summer we go to the Baltic Sea.

cards.title: man: people in general
cards.body: man means one, you or people in general. It is not Mann (the man). Man always takes the same verb form as er and sie: man schwimmt, man trinkt, man spielt. Say it like this: man is a pronoun for everybody, and its verb ends in -t.

examples.en: In the park people play football.
In the café people drink coffee.

cards.more: Pretend man is a secret twin of er. When you talk about one person you say er schwimmt. When you talk about everybody you say man schwimmt. The verb looks exactly the same. So you only need to remember one thing: after man, the verb ends in -t, just like after er and sie. The word man has one n. The word Mann with two n means a male person. Say it out loud: man schwimmt, man spielt.
cards.lead: In the last card you learned the places. Now you learn the little word that lets you talk about everybody there: man. It is a pronoun like er, and the verb after it is easy to guess.

deeper.text: Man has no plural and no gender. It is always one little word, and the verb is always singular. In English you say you, one or they for the same idea: In Spain they eat late. In German you simply say man. Never write man with a capital letter in the middle of a sentence.

cards.title: Three new holiday verbs: wandern, campen, faulenzen
cards.body: Three new verbs for a holiday, all regular: wandern (to hike), campen (to camp) and faulenzen (to laze around, do nothing). Take the stem and add the ending as usual. After man, use the -t form: man wandert, man campt, man faulenzt.

examples.de: Im Sommer campt man am See.
examples.en: In summer people camp at the lake.
Ben lazes around at the beach.

cards.more: Think of three lazy or active holiday friends. One walks a lot: wandern. One sleeps in a tent: campen. One does nothing all day: faulenzen. They are all regular, so the endings work like the verbs you know, such as spielen. Two forms look a little different, because the stem wander already ends in -er: ich wandere (wander + e) and wir wandern, with only -n. For the rest, just add the usual endings.
cards.lead: Now you have places and the word man. What is missing are verbs to go with them. The three new verbs follow the endings you already know, so you can use them with man at once.

deeper.text: With du and er, faulenzen ends the same way: du faulenzt, er faulenzt, because the stem already ends in a hissing sound. Wandern is a verb of movement and you can use it for walking tours of several hours. Faulenzen is the opposite: no plans, no clock, just a deck chair.

example.en: On Sunday people like to laze around.

cards.title: man + can, may, must: the bracket again
cards.body: With man, the modal verb takes the er/sie form too: man kann, man darf, man muss. The modal stands in part 2 and the infinitive waits at the very end. nicht dürfen means forbidden. Careful: man kann, never man können.

examples.en: At the lake you can swim.

examples.de: Im Wald darf man nicht campen.
examples.en: In the forest you may not camp.

cards.more: A bracket has a left side and a right side. The left side is the modal in the second place: kann, darf or muss. The right side is the infinitive at the very end. Everything else sits in between. With man, the modal looks like it does after er: man kann, man darf, man muss. Do not use können with man, because man is one little word, so the verb is singular. Think: Man kann. Er kann. Same!
cards.lead: You know the modal bracket from chapter 5. In this card you combine it with man, so you can say what is allowed, what is forbidden and what is a must in a holiday place.

deeper.text: The two sides of the bracket never move. If you put the place first, the modal still stays in part 2 and man comes right after it. That is why Am See kann man baden is correct. A sign often uses darf nicht to say that something is forbidden, like Hier darf man nicht campen.

example.de: Am Strand darf man nicht rauchen.
example.en: You may not smoke on the beach.

cards.title: Ask with man: Was kann man hier machen?
cards.body: To ask what is possible, use a W-question with man. The question word is first, the modal is in part 2, man comes next, and the infinitive is last. Answer with the same pattern. To learn a word, ask Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch?

examples.why: Was kann man ...? = what is possible?
Wo kann man ...? = where is it possible?

examples.de: Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch?
examples.en: How do you say that in German?
examples.why: A handy question for every learner. Learn it as one piece.

rows: Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch?

cards.more: When you arrive at a holiday place you ask the people there: What can one do here? In German you ask Was kann man hier machen? Then you listen for the answer: Man kann wandern. Notice that the answer uses man too, and the question word just takes the first place in the question. For words you do not know, ask Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch? and point at the thing.
cards.lead: After statements, here come the questions. A W-question starts with the question word, then the verb, so the new part is only that man follows the verb like a subject.

deeper.text: In a question with a modal, the order is question word, modal, subject, middle, infinitive. With man that gives Was kann man machen? You hear this question at every tourist office. The answer can be short, with just the place and the verb: Am Meer kann man schwimmen.

cards.title: man or du? Tips for a visit
cards.body: Use du when you talk to one person. Use man for a general tip or rule that is true for everybody, also about a country. Ferien (holidays) is always plural, so there is no singular: in den Ferien.

examples.de: In Deutschland isst man abends oft Brot.
examples.en: In Germany people often eat bread in the evening.

examples.de: In den Ferien kann man faulenzen.
examples.en: In the holidays you can laze around.

cards.more: Imagine you tell your friend Mira: Du kannst heute faulenzen. That is a tip only for her. Now imagine you tell a visitor about a country: In Deutschland isst man abends oft Brot. That is true for everybody there, so you use man. A simple test: could you say people or one in English? Then use man. Could you say you to one person you know? Then use du.
cards.lead: You now have two ways to say you. The last card compares them, so you choose the right one for a tip about one person and for a rule about a country.

deeper.text: In English you often say you for both ideas: You can swim here. In German you have to decide. Du talks to a person you know. Man is for signs, rules and customs. Ferien is plural only, like the English holidays, so you say die Ferien and the verb has no singular partner.

lessons.title: Packing for a trip: why? denn
lessons.goal: Pack a suitcase, say what you take and give the reason with denn, and ask Warum?

grammar.point: denn joins two sentences and gives a reason. It stands in position 0 like und, oder and aber, so the second sentence keeps normal order: subject, then verb.
grammar.oneLine: Ich nehme einen Regenschirm mit, denn es regnet. Warum nimmst du einen Rucksack mit?

mistake.wrong: Ich nehme einen Regenschirm mit, denn regnet es.
mistake.right: Ich nehme einen Regenschirm mit, denn es regnet.
mistake.why: After denn the sentence is a normal statement: the subject comes first and the verb second.

terms.meaning: a little word that means because and gives a reason
a word that joins two sentences, like und, oder, aber, denn
a place before the sentence: the word does not change the order inside the sentence
two nouns glued together, like Reise + Tasche; the last part gives the article

cards.title: Before we start: what do you take, and why?
cards.body: Before a trip you pack a suitcase, and friends ask you why you take something. Today you say what you take and give the reason with denn. You know und, oder and aber from chapter 7: they join two sentences and the second sentence stays normal. denn works the same way.

examples.de: Ich bleibe zu Hause, aber ich arbeite nicht.
examples.en: I stay at home, but I do not work.
examples.why: You know this already: aber + a normal sentence.

examples.de: Ich nehme einen Regenschirm mit, denn es regnet.
examples.en: I take an umbrella, because it is raining.
examples.why: New today: denn + a normal sentence gives the reason.

examples.de: Warum nimmst du einen Rucksack mit?
examples.en: Why are you taking a backpack?
examples.why: New today: Warum? asks for the reason.

steps: You already know: und, oder and aber join two sentences (chapter 7) and separable verbs like mitnehmen (chapter 6)
New today: ten travel things, Warum? and denn with a reason
By the end you can: say what you take on a trip and why, and say what people need for a journey
cards.more: Suppose your friend sees an umbrella in your bag. She asks Warum? (why?). You answer with a reason: it is raining. In German you join the two ideas with a little word, denn. You use it like aber: it stands between the two sentences, with a comma in front, and the second sentence is just a normal sentence. Today you also learn ten things you put in a suitcase.

cards.title: Travel gear: der Koffer, der Rucksack
cards.body: Ten things for a trip. Learn each noun with its article and plural. A tip for compound nouns: the article comes from the last word. Reise + Tasche: die Tasche, so die Reisetasche. Regen + Schirm: der Schirm, so der Regenschirm.

examples.why: Reise + Tasche: die Tasche, so die Reisetasche.
Regen + Schirm: der Schirm, so der Regenschirm.

cards.more: A compound noun is two nouns glued together. The glue holds, and the last piece decides the article. Think of a train: the last carriage gives the direction. Reise + Tasche: Tasche is die, so die Reisetasche. Reise + Pass: Pass is der, so der Reisepass. When you meet a long new word, look at the end first, find the last part and use its article. This saves you from learning many articles one by one.
cards.lead: The intro gave you the idea of packing. Here are the ten things for your suitcase. You also learn a trick that tells you the article of long compound words from their last part.

deeper.text: The trick works for almost every compound noun. Sonnenbrille ends in Brille, which is die, so die Sonnenbrille. Always check the last part. The first part only gives the meaning: a Reisetasche is a bag for a trip, a Reisepass is a passport for a trip.

cards.title: What do you take? mitnehmen + accusative
cards.body: mitnehmen means to take with you. It is a separable verb: Ich nehme einen Koffer mit. The thing you take is the object, so it takes the accusative: der becomes den or einen. Die, das and the plural stay the same.

examples.en: I take a suitcase with me.
Mira takes a camera with her.
We take two tents with us.
examples.why: plural: no article needed after zwei

cards.more: The thing that you take is the one who gets taken, so it is the object, and objects use the accusative. You already know this from chapter 4: only der changes. Der Koffer becomes einen Koffer. Die Kamera stays eine Kamera. Das Zelt stays ein Zelt. The little word mit jumps to the end of the sentence, like the end piece of a bracket. Before it, nehmen changes to nimmst and nimmt with du and er.
cards.lead: You can name the things. Now you say what you take. This is the accusative again, with a separable verb, so look at the end of the sentence for mit.

deeper.text: With du and er, nehmen changes its vowel: du nimmst, er nimmt. This is the same change as in essen and sehen. The prefix mit goes to the end, so the sentence has a bracket: nimmt ... mit. It is just like Ich stehe um sieben auf.

example.en: You take a hat with you.

cards.title: Warum? Asking for a reason
cards.body: Warum? means why. It is a W-question, so the verb comes second: Warum nimmst du einen Rucksack mit? Answer with a short reason sentence. For now, only learn the reason words with denn, in the next card.

examples.de: Warum nimmst du einen Hut mit?
examples.en: Why are you taking a hat?
Why are you staying at home?
Why is Ben going to Vienna?

rows: Warum nimmst du einen Hut mit?

cards.more: Warum is a question word like wo or wann. It always stands first, and the verb takes the second place, exactly as in all W-questions. Then you listen for a short reason: Es ist heiß. Ich bin müde. The reason can be a whole little sentence. You do not need any new grammar to answer, only a normal sentence. Later you will join the question and the answer with denn.
cards.lead: You can say what you take. Now you learn to ask why someone takes it. The question word Warum follows the W-question rule you know from chapter 1.

deeper.text: A reason is a full sentence with a subject and a verb: Es ist heiß. Die Stadt ist schön. Ich bin müde. You do not need to repeat the whole question in your answer. In everyday speech people often answer with just the reason sentence, and that is fine.

cards.title: denn: because, with normal word order
cards.body: denn means because and gives a reason. Put a comma before it. After denn the sentence stays normal: the subject comes first and the verb second. denn stands outside the sentence, in position 0, like aber.

examples.de: Ich nehme einen Regenschirm mit, denn es regnet.
examples.en: I take an umbrella, because it is raining.

examples.de: Wir bleiben zu Hause, denn es ist kalt.
examples.en: We stay at home, because it is cold.

examples.de: Mira nimmt eine Sonnenbrille mit, denn es ist heiß.
examples.en: Mira takes sunglasses with her, because it is hot.

steps: Write sentence 1 as usual
Add a comma and denn
Write sentence 2 as a normal sentence: subject first, verb second
cards.more: Build the sentence in three pieces. Piece one is a normal sentence. Piece two is a comma and the word denn. Piece three is another normal sentence, with the subject first and the verb right after it. Read it aloud and it sounds like English: I take an umbrella, because it is raining. The word denn does not change anything in the second sentence. It stands outside, like a little bridge.
cards.lead: The question Warum? needs an answer. The answer can be one sentence with denn: it joins your action and your reason in one go, and the word order stays easy.

deeper.text: denn answers the question Warum? The denn part always comes second: first the action, then the reason. It never starts the sentence. The word order after denn is always subject, verb. That makes denn the easiest because-word in German. Other because-words are harder, and you meet them later.

example.de: Ben bleibt zu Hause, denn er ist müde.
example.en: Ben stays at home, because he is tired.

cards.title: denn like und, aber, oder
cards.body: denn belongs to a small family: und, oder, aber, denn. Each one joins two sentences. After each one, the second sentence keeps its normal order: subject, then verb. Other because-words send the verb to the end, but you only meet them later.

examples.de: Ich nehme einen Koffer mit, und Ben nimmt einen Rucksack mit.
examples.en: I take a suitcase and Ben takes a backpack.

examples.de: Ich habe eine Kamera, aber ich habe kein Zelt.
examples.en: I have a camera, but I do not have a tent.

examples.de: Ich bleibe zu Hause, denn ich bin müde.
examples.en: I stay at home, because I am tired.

cards.more: Four little words, one job: they connect two sentences. Und adds, oder gives a choice, aber shows a contrast and denn gives a reason. They all stand at the very beginning of the second sentence, but they do not count as a place in the sentence. So after them you simply say who does something and what. You do not need to move anything around. That is why you can use them without thinking.
cards.lead: You now know denn. This card puts it next to und, oder and aber, so you see the pattern that all four little words share and choose the right one.

deeper.text: These four words sit in position 0: before the subject, not inside the sentence. The verb stays in position 2 as usual. This is why you can always check yourself: after und, oder, aber or denn, read the next two words and make sure they are the subject and then the verb.

example.de: Möchtest du baden, oder möchtest du wandern?
example.en: Do you want to swim, or do you want to hike?

cards.title: Pack for a purpose: Was braucht man?
cards.body: brauchen means to need and takes the accusative. Combine it with man: Man braucht einen Reisepass. Für eine Reise braucht man einen Reisepass. You can add a reason: Man braucht ein Ticket, denn man fährt mit dem Zug.

examples.de: Für eine Reise braucht man einen Reisepass.
examples.en: For a trip you need a passport.

examples.de: Am Strand braucht man eine Sonnenbrille, denn es ist heiß.
examples.en: At the beach you need sunglasses, because it is hot.

examples.de: Im Zug braucht man ein Ticket, denn man muss bezahlen.
examples.en: On the train you need a ticket, because you have to pay.
examples.why: a reason can use man too

cards.more: Imagine you write a packing list. For each place you ask: what does one need? At the beach: sunglasses, because it is hot. In the mountains: a backpack, because you hike a lot. On the train: a ticket, because you have to pay. Each line has the same pieces: the place, braucht man, the thing in the accusative and a reason after denn. The verb brauchen is regular, and man takes the er/sie form: man braucht.
cards.lead: This card puts everything together: man from lesson 1, the accusative with things, and denn for the reason. It also gives you a way to write a short packing list.

deeper.text: Both parts of the sentence can start with the place. In Am Strand braucht man eine Sonnenbrille, the verb stays in part 2 and man follows it. The reason after denn begins with its own subject. Short packing lists with a reason are common on holiday websites.

example.de: In den Bergen braucht man einen Rucksack, denn man wandert viel.
example.en: In the mountains you need a backpack, because you hike a lot.

lessons.title: A city tour: wer, wen, wem, was?
lessons.goal: Plan a city tour with friends: ask about people and things with the right question word, and make a suggestion with Wollen wir ...?

grammar.point: The question word shows the job in the sentence: wer is the person who does it, wen the person who gets it, wem the person after mit, bei, von or zu, and was a thing.
grammar.oneLine: Wer macht die Führung? Wen fragen wir? Mit wem machst du die Stadtrundfahrt?

mistake.why: The person is the object, so the question word is wen. wer asks for the doer.

terms.meaning: a word like wer, wen, wem, was that starts a question
the doer in the sentence: the one who does something
the person or thing that gets the action
the form after mit, bei, von, zu and verbs like gefallen: mit dem Mann

cards.title: Before we start: planning a city tour together
cards.body: On holiday you often plan a day in a city with friends: who does the tour, whom do we ask, who comes with us? Today you ask these questions with the right question word. You know Wen besuchst du? and Mit wem arbeitest du? Now you meet the whole family: wer, wen, wem and was.

examples.why: You know this already: wen asks for a person who is the object.

examples.en: Who is doing the guided tour?
examples.why: New today: wer asks for the person who does something.

examples.de: Mit wem machst du die Stadtrundfahrt?
examples.en: With whom are you doing the city tour?
examples.why: New today: wem comes after mit, bei, von and zu.

steps: You already know: Wen besuchst du? (chapter 6) and Mit wem arbeitest du? (chapter 7)
New today: wer, wen, wem and was side by side, ten words for a city tour, and Wollen wir ...?
By the end you can: ask who or what, answer with the right form, and suggest a city tour to a friend
cards.more: Imagine four friends and one city. Someone has to do the guided tour, someone has to buy the tickets, and you want to know who comes with you. Each question needs a different little word in German, depending on the job of the person in the sentence. You already know two of them, wen and wem. Today you add wer and was, and you learn how to choose between all four.

cards.title: City sights: die Altstadt, das Schloss, der Dom
cards.body: Ten words for a city tour. Nine are nouns, so learn each with its article and its plural. The verb besichtigen means to visit a sight: Wir besichtigen das Schloss. Compound nouns take the article of the last part: Stadt + Plan = der Plan, so der Stadtplan.

examples.why: die Altstadt: the last part is die Stadt
Stadt + Plan: der Plan, so der Stadtplan

cards.more: Picture a postcard of a big old city. In the middle is the Altstadt, the old town. On a hill there is a Schloss or a Burg, and in a square there is a big Dom. At the end of the day you look at the Stadtplan. Learn each word with its article, and use the last part of a compound noun to find it. The verb besichtigen is for sights only. For a friend you simply visit: besuchen.
cards.lead: The intro asked who and what. To ask about a city tour you need the words for the city itself. Here are the ten words, with their articles and plurals.

deeper.text: Besichtigen starts with the part be-, so it is not separable. The stress is on the second part, and the verb keeps its first part in every form: ich besichtige, du besichtigst, er besichtigt. Use besuchen for people and besichtigen for places like a castle or a cathedral.

cards.title: wer and was: the subject
cards.body: wer asks for a person who does something. was asks for a thing. Both go with the subject. After wer, the verb takes the er/sie form: Wer besichtigt das Schloss? Answer with the name or the thing.

examples.why: wer = a person who does it

examples.en: Who is doing the city tour?

cards.more: Wer means who. Use it when you ask for the person who does something, like the doer. The verb after wer looks like the verb after er: wer macht, wer besichtigt, wer kommt. Was means what. Use it for things. The question Was ist das? is the most useful question on a holiday: you point at something and ask. The answer begins with Das ist ...
cards.lead: You know wer from the very first chapter, and was from the questions with machen. This card puts them together: both ask for the subject of the sentence, one for a person and one for a thing.

deeper.text: Wer is always singular in German, even if you expect several people. That is why the verb is in the er/sie form: Wer kommt mit? You then answer with whatever number is true: Mira und Ben kommen mit. The question uses singular, the answer can be plural.

cards.title: wen and was: the object
cards.body: wen asks for a person who is the object, in the accusative. Answer with den, einen or meinen for masculine words: Wen siehst du? Den Mann. Names do not change: Wen besuchst du? Leon. was also asks for things as the object.

examples.why: wen = a person as the object
was = a thing as the object

cards.more: Think of the sentence as a little story. Somebody does something, and somebody or something gets it. The one who gets it is the object. If it is a person, ask wen. If it is a thing, ask was. The answer for a masculine person uses den: den Mann, einen Freund. Women and names do not change: Frau Weber, Leon, Anna. The word was is the same as before, so you only have to learn wen.
cards.lead: Now you ask for the person or thing that gets the action. Here wen and was work together with the accusative, which you know from chapter 4 and chapter 6.

deeper.text: In the question the subject comes after the verb: Wen fragen wir? Wir is the subject, so the question word wen must be the object. A quick test: if you can answer with ihn or sie (him or her), you ask wen. Wen besuchst du? Ich besuche ihn. This is the same pattern as mich, dich and ihn.

cards.title: wem: with, at, from, to someone
cards.body: wem asks for a person in the dative. It comes after mit, bei, von and zu: Mit wem machst du die Führung? Answer with the dative: mit dem Mann, mit meiner Schwester, mit Leon. The same wem also goes with gefallen and helfen.

examples.de: Mit wem machst du die Führung?
examples.en: With whom are you doing the guided tour?

examples.why: bei wem: answer Bei meiner Schwester.

rows: Mit wem machst du die Führung?

cards.more: Some small words always want a person in the dative: mit, bei, von and zu. You know them from chapter 7. To ask about that person, use wem and put the small word in front: Mit wem? Bei wem? Von wem? Zu wem? The answer uses the dative, like mit dem Mann or mit meiner Schwester. Names do not change: Mit Leon. Chapter 11 showed two verbs that also want the dative: Wem gefällt die Altstadt? Mir. Wem hilfst du? Meiner Freundin.
cards.lead: You already know wem from Mit wem? in chapter 7. Here you see it with more small words and with the verbs from the shop chapter, so you hear the pattern in many places.

deeper.text: The preposition always comes first, before wem, as one unit: Mit wem, Bei wem. Do not split them. With gefallen and helfen there is no preposition, wem stands alone at the start. Answer with a dative pronoun: mir, dir, ihm, ihr, uns, euch, ihnen, or with a dative noun group.

cards.title: Four question words side by side
cards.body: Choose in three steps: what is the person or thing doing in the sentence? Is it a person or a thing? Then pick. wer: the person who does it. wen: the person who gets it. wem: the person with, at, from or to whom. was: a thing, as the doer or as the object.

examples.de: Mit wem besichtigst du das Schloss?
examples.en: With whom do you visit the castle?

steps: Find the job of the person or thing in your sentence: doer, receiver or after mit, bei, von, zu
Decide: person or thing?
Pick the word: wer, wen, wem or was
cards.more: Imagine four boxes. In the first box you put the doer, the person who does something: wer. In the second box you put the person who gets the action: wen. In the third box you put the person after mit, bei, von or zu: wem. In the fourth box go all things: was. Before you ask, look at your sentence and ask yourself which box the person belongs in. Then take the little word from that box.
cards.lead: You now know four question words, each from a different lesson or card. This card puts them in one table, so you can decide which one fits your question.

deeper.text: The three person words are three cases of one question: wer is the nominative, wen the accusative and wem the dative. Was does not change between subject and object. If you are not sure, translate your answer: er, ihn or ihm? That tells you wer, wen or wem.

cards.title: Suggest a city tour: Wollen wir ...?
cards.body: To suggest something, ask a yes/no question with wollen: Wollen wir die Altstadt besichtigen? You can also say Wir können eine Stadtrundfahrt machen. Learn these as pieces: Ich habe einen Vorschlag. Gute Idee! Das ist ein guter Vorschlag!

examples.en: Shall we visit the old town?
We can do a city tour.

examples.why: learn ein guter Vorschlag as one piece

rows: Ich habe einen Vorschlag: Wollen wir die Altstadt besichtigen?

cards.more: In English you say Shall we ...? or Why don't we ...? In German you can say Wollen wir ...? It is a yes/no question with the verb first, then wir, and the infinitive at the end: Wollen wir die Altstadt besichtigen? The friend answers with Gute Idee! or Das ist ein guter Vorschlag! You do not need to know why guter has an -er ending yet. Learn the whole piece. You will meet the rule later.
cards.lead: The questions about people and things help you plan. The last step is to make a suggestion and react to one, as friends do when they plan a day in a city.

deeper.text: Wollen wir ...? asks for the other person's opinion, so it sounds friendly. With Wir können ... you say what is possible. Both use the modal bracket: the modal stands in part 1 or 2, the infinitive at the end. Mira, Ben and Leon use these exact pieces to plan a Saturday in a city they visit together.

lessons.title: Which way? Question words, compass points and the route
lessons.goal: Pick the right question word for any information, say where a city is, and understand a train route.

grammar.point: All question words stand in part 1 and the verb in part 2. Wo asks for a place, wohin for a direction, woher for an origin.
grammar.oneLine: Wo bist du? Wohin fährst du? Woher kommst du? Place, direction, origin.

mistake.right: Wohin fährst du? Ich fahre nach Berlin.
mistake.why: Wo asks for the place where you are. Wohin asks for the direction you go.

terms.meaning: a word like wer, was or wohin that starts a question and asks for one piece of information
one of the four directions: Norden, Süden, Osten, Westen
a verb that splits in a statement, like umsteigen: ich steige um

cards.title: Before we start: how do I get there?
cards.body: A real moment: you are at the station and need to know where the train goes and when. In chapter 3 you asked Wo ist ...? Today you pick the right question word for any information, and you read a train timetable.

examples.why: You know this: wo asks for a place.
New today: wohin asks for a direction.

examples.de: Wann fährt der Zug nach München?
examples.en: When does the train to Munich leave?
examples.why: New today: wann asks for a time.

steps: You already know: Wo wohnst du? and Woher kommst du?
New today: wohin, compass points and a train timetable.
By the end you can: ask Wohin fährst du? and say Der Zug fährt um 9 Uhr ab.
cards.more: Think of question words as little tools in a toolbox. Wo is the tool for a place, wohin is for a direction, wann is for a time. If you grab the wrong tool, you get the wrong answer. Today you learn the whole toolbox on one page, and then you practise the three tools you will need most at a station. Each card is short, with a table and colours to help you see the pattern. No new verb forms are needed today.

cards.title: Compass points: der Norden, der Süden, der Osten, der Westen
cards.body: The four compass points are masculine: der Norden, der Süden, der Osten, der Westen. They have no plural. To say where a city is, use im (in + dem): Hamburg liegt im Norden. For the direction of travel, learn the chunk in Richtung Norden.

examples.de: Der Zug fährt in Richtung Norden.
examples.en: The train goes towards the north.

cards.more: Imagine a map with four doors: north at the top, south at the bottom, east on the right, west on the left. Each door has a masculine name, so each one wears im when you say a city is in that part of the country. Step 1: say the city. Step 2: say liegt. Step 3: say im and the door name. That is it. For going towards a direction, just remember the whole chunk in Richtung Norden and copy it.
cards.lead: In chapter 9 you learned that liegen says where something is. Now you use it for cities. This card gives you the four compass points and one small chunk for the direction a train goes.

deeper.text: English says in the north with in the. German squeezes in dem into one word, im, because all four compass points are masculine. That is the same im you already use for im Sommer and im Mai. The pattern never changes: a city, liegt, im, and the compass point.

cards.title: All the question words in one table
cards.body: Every question word goes in part 1, and the verb stays in part 2. Pick the word by the information you want: a person, a thing, a place, a direction, an origin, a time, a way, an amount, a choice or a reason.

examples.why: wer asks for a person (the subject).

examples.en: How long does the trip take?
examples.why: Wie lange asks for a length of time.

cards.more: Before you ask, decide what you want to know. Is it a person? Use wer. A thing? Use was. A place? Use wo. Each wish has one word, like keys on a ring. Put the key in part 1. Then the verb goes right behind it in part 2, and the rest of the sentence follows. If you cannot find the right key, look at the table again. After a few days you will grab the right key without thinking.
cards.lead: You already know many question words from earlier chapters. This card puts them all in one table, so you can see the whole toolbox at once and choose the right word for the information you want.

deeper.text: In every German question the question word is part 1 and the verb is part 2, exactly as in a statement. The subject comes after the verb. So you only have to choose one word. Ask yourself first: what do I want to know? Then pick the row in the table. Welcher changes its ending, but today you only need welcher in front of a masculine noun like Zug.

example.en: Why is Mira going to Munich?

cards.title: wo, wohin, woher: place, direction, origin
cards.body: Three small words, three different jobs. Wo asks where you are. Wohin asks where you are going. Woher asks where you come from. The answer shows the job: in + place, nach + city or zu + place, aus + place.
cards.more: Picture a trip as three dots on a line: where you started, where you are going, and where you are right now. Woher points back to the start. Wohin points forward to the goal. Wo points at the dot where you stand. Before you ask, say to yourself: back, forward or here? Then pick woher, wohin or wo. The little answer words match: aus for the start, nach for the goal, in for the place.
cards.lead: In chapter 1 you learned wo and woher. The new word on this card is wohin. It sits between them: wo is here, wohin is on the way there, woher is where it started.

deeper.text: Many English speakers say where for all three jobs: Where do you go? Where are you? Where do you come from? German splits where into three words, so the question already tells the other person which answer you want. Use three steps: am I there already, am I going there, or am I coming from there? That choice gives you wo, wohin or woher.

example.en: Ben is going to the station.

cards.title: A timetable: Abfahrt, Ankunft, Gleis, Verbindung
cards.body: A departure board shows the train, the direction, the platform, the Abfahrt (departure) and the Ankunft (arrival). Learn three whole chunks: Wann fährt der Zug ab? Wann kommt der Zug an? Auf Gleis 5. They come from the verbs abfahren and ankommen.

examples.de: Der Zug fährt um 9 Uhr auf Gleis 5 ab.
examples.en: The train leaves at 9 o'clock from platform 5.

examples.de: Der Zug kommt um 15 Uhr an.

cards.more: Think of the departure board like a small table with five columns. Each column answers one question: which train, where to, which platform, when does it go, when does it arrive. You copy the question Wann fährt der Zug ab? exactly as it is, like a ready-made phrase. The same goes for Wann kommt der Zug an? and Auf Gleis 5. You do not build them yourself yet. Just use them like building blocks at the station.
cards.lead: You can already ask wohin and wann. On this card you use them at the station. The new words are Abfahrt, Ankunft, Gleis and Verbindung, plus two chunks you can copy whole.

deeper.text: Abfahrt and Ankunft are nouns made from the verbs abfahren and ankommen. In a sentence the verb splits: the main part is in part 2 and the little word ab or an waits at the end, just like aufstehen in chapter 6. A Verbindung is one way to get from A to B, often with a change on the way. You do not have to learn clock forms: full hours are enough.

cards.title: Change trains: umsteigen
cards.body: Umsteigen means to change trains. It is a separable verb like aufstehen: ich steige um, with um at the end. With a modal it stays whole at the end: Ich muss umsteigen. In the Perfekt it uses sein: ich bin umgestiegen.

examples.why: Present: um goes to the end.

examples.en: Where do I have to change?
examples.why: Modal: the infinitive is whole at the end.
sein: it is a change of place.

cards.more: Imagine a verb with a small tail, um. In a normal sentence, the tail jumps to the very end: Ich steige in Hannover um. With a modal helper, the verb keeps its tail on and goes whole to the end: Ich muss umsteigen. In the Perfekt you use sein, because changing trains is moving. Step 1: find the sentence type. Step 2: put the tail or the whole verb at the end.
cards.lead: The last card gave you the station chunks. This card adds one very useful verb for long trips: umsteigen. You already know separable verbs and modals, so you only learn how they fit together here.

deeper.text: A separable verb splits in a normal statement: the verb stays in part 2 and um goes to the end. With a modal, the modal stands in part 2 and the verb waits whole at the end, so you do not split it. In the Perfekt, umsteigen uses sein, because you move from one train to another. The participle is umgestiegen, with ge in the middle.

example.en: Ben has to change in Hannover.

cards.title: Give a route in steps
cards.body: To describe a route, tell it in order with zuerst, dann and danach. Each word takes position 1, so the verb follows right behind it in part 2. Ask for facts with Wie lange dauert die Fahrt? and Wie viele Stunden?

examples.de: Zuerst fahre ich mit dem Zug von Hamburg nach Hannover.
examples.en: First I take the train from Hamburg to Hannover.
After that I go to Munich.

rows: Zuerst fahre ich von Hamburg nach Hannover.

cards.more: A route is a story with three scenes: first, then, after that. Each scene starts with a little time word. After that word comes the verb, because the verb always sits in part 2. So you never say Zuerst ich fahre. You say Zuerst fahre ich. When you want to know how long it lasts, ask Wie lange dauert die Fahrt? and listen for a number of hours. Short, ordered, easy to follow.
cards.lead: You know zuerst, dann and danach from chapter 10. Now you use them to tell a whole route. After each of these words the verb comes next, so the order you learned stays the same.

deeper.text: These three words are time words in position 1, so the verb is always next and the subject comes after it. That means Zuerst fahre ich, not Zuerst ich fahre. A route needs only these three sentences. You can ask about the trip with the question words from the table: Wie lange dauert die Fahrt? Wie viele Stunden dauert sie? Welcher Zug fährt nach Köln?

example.en: How many hours does the trip take?

lessons.title: When? Weather and the time words ab, seit, in, vor, nach
lessons.goal: Say when, since when and in how long, and describe the weather.

grammar.point: Seit, ab, in, vor, nach and an are followed by the dative: seit drei Tagen, ab Montag, in einer Woche, vor dem Frühstück, nach der Arbeit, am Montag.
grammar.oneLine: Seit drei Tagen regnet es. Ab Montag ist es kalt. Seit + dative, plural noun + n.

terms.meaning: the form after words like seit, ab, in, vor and nach: dem, der, dem, den + n
a small word like seit or in that stands before a noun and gives time or place
the empty word es, as in Es regnet

cards.title: Before we start: when does the sun come out?
cards.body: A real moment: you plan a trip and want to know the weather. When does it get warm? Since when does it rain? In chapter 5 you said von Montag bis Freitag. Today you learn more small time words: seit, ab, in, vor and nach, and you talk about the weather.

examples.de: Ich arbeite von Montag bis Freitag.
examples.en: I work from Monday to Friday.
It has been raining for a week.

examples.why: New today: ab = from then on.

steps: You already know: von Montag bis Freitag and the dative (dem, der, dem, den).
New today: seit, ab, in, vor, nach and the weather words.
By the end you can: say Seit zwei Tagen regnet es. Ab Montag scheint die Sonne.
cards.more: Time words are like little signposts. Von and bis show a stretch with a start and an end. Today you meet signposts that point back (seit, vor), forward (ab, in) or to a moment (nach). Each one is followed by the dative, which you already know from chapter 7. You will also learn how to say that it rains, that the sun shines and how warm it is. Take it one card at a time.

cards.title: Weather: Wie ist das Wetter?
cards.body: For the weather German uses es as an empty subject, like English it: Es regnet. With the sun, the real subject is die Sonne: Die Sonne scheint (scheinen: to shine). Use es ist for sonnig, windig and bewölkt. For the temperature learn the chunk Es sind 20 Grad.

examples.why: es = empty subject, like English it.
The real subject is die Sonne.

cards.more: Think of es as a quiet actor who stands on stage so that the sentence is not empty. Es regnet: the rain falls, and es is the actor. Es schneit: the same for snow. When something real does the job, you name it, like die Sonne in Die Sonne scheint. For the temperature, copy the chunk Es sind 20 Grad. Say the number you like in front of Grad, and Grad stays the same.
cards.lead: You know das Wetter and regnen from earlier chapters. This card adds the weather nouns, three adjectives and the empty word es. You can say it in one short sentence.

deeper.text: In English you say it rains. German does the same: es regnet. The word es has no meaning here. It only fills the subject slot, because a German sentence needs a subject. Es schneit is a chunk for it snows. For the sun there is a real subject, so you say die Sonne scheint. After a number, Grad does not change: zehn Grad.

cards.title: seit + dative: since when?
cards.body: Seit says that something started in the past and is still going on now. It uses the dative and the present tense: Es regnet seit drei Tagen. The question is Seit wann? Plural nouns add -n after seit: seit drei Tagen. Use dem, einer or einem before a singular noun.

examples.en: It has been raining for a week.

examples.de: Ich lerne seit einem Monat Deutsch.
examples.en: I have been learning German for a month.

examples.de: Seit dem Frühling ist es warm.
examples.en: It has been warm since spring.

cards.more: Seit is like a ruler that starts at a point in the past and runs all the way to now. Because it is still running, the verb stays in the present. Ask Seit wann? and answer with seit plus the length or the start: seit drei Tagen, seit dem Frühling. The word after seit needs the dative ending. For a plural, add -n to the noun, so Tage becomes Tagen. For one week, say seit einer Woche.
cards.lead: You know seit and Seit wann? from earlier. Now you use seit with the dative in full. You already know the dative from chapter 7, so only the plural -n may feel new.

deeper.text: English says has been raining for a week. German uses the plain present: es regnet seit einer Woche. The thing is not finished, so you do not need the Perfekt. After seit comes the dative, just as after mit or bei. Plural nouns get an extra -n: Tage becomes Tagen, but Wochen already ends in -n and stays Wochen.

example.en: Since when has it been raining?

cards.title: ab: from ... on
cards.body: Ab means from this moment on, into the future. After weekdays and morgen it has no article: ab Montag, ab morgen. With a date, use ab dem: ab dem 1. Mai. With a time, use the number: ab 8 Uhr. The verb follows right behind it.

examples.de: Ab dem 1. Mai ist es warm.

cards.more: Draw a line on paper. Mark today on it. Seit points backwards from today. Ab points forwards: the line starts at a future point and keeps going. So ab Montag means Monday and every day after. You do not need a little word before Montag or morgen. With a date, keep dem: ab dem 1. Mai. Copy the chunk Ab Montag ist es kalt and swap the weekday when you need to.
cards.lead: On the last card seit looked back. Ab looks forward. It is the signpost for something that starts at a point in the future and goes on. You already know weekdays from chapter 2 and dates from chapter 6.

deeper.text: Seit and ab are mirror images. Seit starts in the past and runs to now. Ab starts at a future point and runs onward. With weekdays and morgen German drops the article: ab Montag. With a date it keeps the dative dem, and you say ersten when you read 1. aloud. Ab Montag ist es kalt is a chunk you can copy.

cards.title: in: in a week, in two days
cards.body: In + time + dative says how long from now until something happens: In einer Woche fahre ich nach München. In zwei Tagen scheint die Sonne. This is different from im Mai or im Sommer, which says during a month or a season.

examples.de: In einer Woche fahre ich nach München.
examples.en: In a week I am going to Munich.

examples.de: In zwei Tagen scheint die Sonne.
examples.en: In two days the sun shines.

rows: In einer Woche fahre ich nach Köln.

cards.more: Imagine a clock that starts counting at this very moment. In einer Woche means: after one week on that clock, something happens. It is a countdown. Months and seasons are different. They are boxes on the calendar, and you stand inside the box: im Mai, im Sommer. So ask yourself: am I counting from now, or naming a box? Counting uses in + einer Woche. A box uses im.
cards.lead: You know in from places and from im Mai. This card shows a second job for in. With a length of time it counts from now. Compare the two uses side by side so you do not mix them.

deeper.text: In English you say in a week for the time from now, and the same in German: in einer Woche. The word after in takes the dative, so you see einer, zwei Tagen and so on. Months and seasons also use in, but they merge with dem into im: im Mai. If you can count the time, use in plus the length. If it is a month, use im.

example.de: In drei Tagen beginnt der Urlaub.
example.en: In three days the holiday starts.

cards.title: vor and nach: before, after, ago
cards.body: Vor means before or ago. Nach means after. Both use the dative: vor dem Frühstück, nach der Arbeit, nach dem Essen. Vor einer Woche means a week ago and goes with war. Nach has two jobs: nach + city (nach Berlin) and nach + a time.

examples.de: Nach der Arbeit lerne ich Deutsch.
Vor einer Woche war ich in Berlin.
examples.en: A week ago I was in Berlin.

rows: Nach der Arbeit lerne ich Deutsch.
Vor einer Woche war ich in Berlin.

cards.more: Vor and nach are like two doors on either side of an event. Before the door is vor, after the door is nach. Because they sit next to a noun, the noun gets its dative: vor dem Frühstück, nach der Arbeit. When you add a length of time, vor looks back: vor einer Woche, a week ago. You cannot use seit for that, because the week is finished. With a city, nach means to: nach Berlin.
cards.lead: In lesson 4 you used nach with a city, as in nach München. Now nach gets a second job, and vor joins it. Both are short signposts, both are followed by the dative, and both are easy to use.

deeper.text: Vor and nach are opposites, like before and after. They work with events like Frühstück and Arbeit, and with lengths of time like einer Woche. With a length of time, vor means ago, and you use war or the Perfekt. With a city, nach means to, and it needs no article. Same word, two jobs. The next word shows you which job it does.

example.de: Nach dem Essen trinke ich Tee.
example.en: After the meal I drink tea.

cards.title: an, seit, ab, in, vor, nach: all six together
cards.body: Six small words, six jobs. Use three steps: is it in the past, now or the future? Past: vor (ago) or seit (still going). Future: ab (starting then) or in (from now). A day or a moment: an (am Montag) or nach (after).

rows: In zwei Tagen scheint die Sonne.
Vor einer Woche war ich in Berlin.
Nach dem Regen scheint die Sonne.

cards.more: Imagine a line of days with today in the middle. To the left lies the past. There you use vor for a point and seit for a stretch that still runs. To the right lies the future. There you use ab for a start and in for a countdown. A single day takes am, as in am Montag. And an event can be a marker, so nach der Arbeit means after it. Pick by the position on the line.
cards.lead: You have met all six words now. This card puts them in one table, so you can see how they fit together. Choosing the right one is a matter of three small steps.

deeper.text: To pick a word, ask where you are on the timeline. If it already happened and is over, use vor. If it started and still goes on, use seit. If it begins later and goes on, use ab. If you count from now, use in. For a day, use am. For after an event, use nach. All six take the dative. You choose once, and the rest of the sentence stays the same.

lessons.title: A postcard, a travel report ... and a look back at A1
lessons.goal: Write a postcard, retell a travel report from key facts, say f, v and w correctly, and see how far you have come in A1.

grammar.point: A postcard uses the present for now and the Perfekt for what happened. To retell a text, list five key facts: Wer? Wohin? Wann? Was? Wie war es?
grammar.oneLine: Das Wetter ist toll. Wir haben viel erlebt. Wir sind mit dem Zug gefahren. Present for now, Perfekt for the past.

mistake.why: fahren is a movement verb, so the Perfekt uses sein, and the destination takes nach.

terms.meaning: the past tense made with haben or sein in part 2 and a participle at the end
one short piece of information in a text: who, where to, when, what, how it was
the verb form at the end of the Perfekt, for example gefahren

cards.title: Before we start: Viele Grüße von der Ostsee!
cards.body: A real moment: you are on holiday and want to send a postcard. What do you write? This is the last lesson of A1, so you also look back at everything you can do now. Today you write a postcard, retell a travel report and practise the sounds f, v and w.

examples.en: Many greetings from the Baltic Sea!
examples.why: You know this: Viele Grüße from chapter 6.

examples.en: We have visited the old town.
examples.why: New use of the Perfekt you know.

examples.en: It has been raining for three days.

steps: You already know: Liebe ..., Viele Grüße and the Perfekt from chapter 10.
New today: a postcard in four parts and a travel report from five key facts.
By the end you can: write a postcard and see how far you have come in A1.
cards.more: This lesson puts together everything you know. A postcard is short, but it uses the present for now and the Perfekt for what happened. You do not learn a new rule today. You use old rules in a new job: you write a card, you tell a story from five key facts, and you finish A1 with a look back. At the end, you will see how much you can already do in German.

cards.title: A postcard in four parts
cards.body:
A postcard is easy when you split it into four parts: a greeting (Liebe Anna,), where you are and the weather, what you did and one wish, and an ending (Viele Grüße
dein Ben). A Briefmarke (stamp) goes on the Postkarte. Keep each part to one or two short sentences.

examples.de: Liebe Anna, wir sind an der Küste.
examples.en: Dear Anna, we are on the coast.

examples.why: Part 2: the weather in the present.

rows: Wir sind in Husum. Das Wetter ist toll.

cards.more: Think of a postcard as a small house with four rooms. Room one is the hello. Room two says where you are and how the weather is. Room three tells one thing you did. Room four says goodbye. Each room needs only one or two short sentences. When you cannot think of what to write, walk through the rooms in order. The frame, Liebe at the top and Viele Grüße at the bottom, is always the same, so you can copy it.
cards.lead: You know Liebe ... and Viele Grüße from chapter 6. This card shows how to put them in a frame and fill the middle with the weather and a short report. New words: die Postkarte, die Briefmarke, die Küste, erleben.

deeper.text: The frame never changes. At the top comes Liebe or Lieber and the name. At the end comes Viele Grüße with no comma, and on the next line dein or deine with your name. In the middle you say where you are and what the weather is like in the present, and then what you did in the Perfekt. A postcard has little space, so each sentence is short and clear.

cards.title: What happened, what is now: Perfekt and present
cards.body: Use the present for what is true now: Das Wetter ist toll. Use the Perfekt for what already happened: haben or sein in part 2, the participle at the end. Movement uses sein: Wir sind gefahren. Where did you sleep? In einer Jugendherberge (youth hostel) or einer Ferienwohnung (holiday flat). Some participles have no ge-: übernachtet, erlebt, besichtigt.

examples.de: Wir haben in einer Jugendherberge übernachtet.
examples.en: We stayed overnight in a youth hostel.

examples.de: Wir sind mit dem Zug gefahren.

rows: Wir sind mit dem Zug gefahren.
Wir haben in einer Ferienwohnung übernachtet.

cards.more: A postcard has two clocks. One clock shows now: the sun shines, the hotel is nice. For this clock you use the present. The other clock shows what already happened: you stayed in a hostel, you travelled by train. For this clock you use the Perfekt: a helper verb in part 2 and the participle at the end. Did you move? Use sein. Did you do something else? Use haben. Some words have no ge-, so learn them whole.
cards.lead: In chapter 10 you learned the Perfekt with haben and sein. This card shows how it works on a postcard next to the present. You also meet two new verbs, übernachten and erleben.

deeper.text: The helper verb sits in part 2 and the participle waits at the very end. If you did something, use haben. If you moved from one place to another, use sein, as with gefahren. A few participles have no ge-, for example übernachtet, erlebt and besichtigt. Learn them as whole words. For the weather today, switch back to the present.

cards.title: A travel report: retell from key facts
cards.body: To retell a text, for example a Reisebericht (travel report), first find five key facts: Wer? Wohin? Wann? Was? Wie war es? Write each fact in two or three words. Then say each fact in one sentence and link the sentences with zuerst, dann and danach.

examples.de: Zuerst ist Ben nach Husum gefahren.
Dann hat er in einer Jugendherberge übernachtet.
examples.en: Then he stayed in a youth hostel.

cards.more: Imagine you have a hand with five fingers. Each finger is one key fact: who, where to, when, what, how was it. You can hold the whole story in one hand. To tell it, point to each finger in order and say one short sentence. Use zuerst for the first finger, dann for the next and danach for the one after. Do not copy whole sentences. Use your own words and the words from the text that you already know.
cards.lead: A long text is easy to retell when you only keep five facts. You know every question word from lesson 4, and zuerst, dann and danach from chapter 10. This card shows the method with a four-sentence report.

deeper.text: A good report ends with how it was, and often with a little thing you bring home: das Souvenir (souvenir). It keeps die Erinnerung (memory) alive. So the last finger of your hand can be: Ich habe ein Souvenir gekauft. Das ist eine schöne Erinnerung. Both sentences use words you know, and they close the story in a warm way.

example.de: Das Souvenir ist eine schöne Erinnerung.
example.en: The souvenir is a nice memory.

cards.title: Holidays in Germany: where to go
cards.body: Many families spend their holiday in Germany. In the north are the Nordsee and the Ostsee, with sea and beaches. In the south are the Alpen, with mountains to hike in. The Schwarzwald is a forest in the south. Berlin and Hamburg are good for city trips.

examples.en: The North Sea is in the north.
In the Black Forest you can hike.

examples.why: Urlaub machen = to take a holiday

cards.more: Imagine a map of Germany with four signs. In the north there is the sea: the Nordsee and the Ostsee. In the south there are mountains: the Alpen. In the middle and the east you find cities such as Berlin, and Hamburg stands in the north. You do not need a new rule to talk about them. You say im Norden or im Süden, and what you can do with man kann. These names are good words for your postcard.
cards.lead: Now you know the compass points from lesson 4 and the holiday words from lesson 1. This card puts them together on a small map of Germany. There is no new grammar, only new place names.

deeper.text: Place names like Nordsee and Ostsee are proper nouns, and with die they are feminine. The Alpen always appear in the plural. You describe where a place is with im Norden or im Süden, and what you do there with man and a modal. All the pieces come from earlier lessons, so you can build your own sentences without learning new rules.

example.de: An der Nordsee kann man baden.
example.en: At the North Sea you can swim.

cards.title: The sounds f, v, w
cards.body: Three letters, two sounds. F is like English f: Fisch, Fahrrad. V in German words also sounds like f: Vater, viel, von. W sounds like English v: Wasser, wir, wohnen, Wald. So wir sounds like English veer, and vier sounds like feer.

examples.de: Wir fahren viel mit dem Fahrrad.
examples.why: w = v, f = f, v = f

examples.de: Von Hamburg nach Wien ist es weit.
examples.en: From Hamburg to Vienna it is far.

cards.more: Say out loud: wir, vier. Wir starts with a buzzing sound, like English v in very. Vier starts with a soft blowing sound, like English f in fish. Written W gives you the buzz. Written V gives you the blow. And the letter F always blows. If you remember one thing, remember that German w is the English v. Then read the words in the table aloud once, slowly, and keep the sounds apart.
cards.lead: You can already read and say many German words. This card gives you one trick for three letters that look like English but sound different. Read the table aloud once and your sound will improve.

deeper.text: The letters v and w are swapped compared with English. German w sounds like English v, and German v sounds like English f. That is why wir and vier sound different, and why Wald and viel are not the same. Loanwords such as Vase keep the English v sound, but you only need to know that as a note. For everyday German words use the table.

cards.title: A look back: what you can do after A1
cards.body: You have finished A1. You can greet people and talk about yourself, buy things, tell time, invite friends, describe your body, your home and your work, talk about the past and travel. The table shows one sentence for each chapter. Next comes A2.

rows: Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.

cards.more: Look at the table as a photo album. Each row is one photo from one chapter, and each photo has one sentence. Cover the German column and read the topic. Can you say a sentence about greetings? About food? About health? If yes, you have learned it. If not, look at the sentence and say it aloud twice. Nothing new is coming on this card, because A1 is done. Next: A2, with longer stories and more freedom.
cards.lead: This is the end of A1. On this card you look back at all twelve chapters and see one sentence from each. There is no new grammar here, only a small proof of how much you can already say.

deeper.text: Twelve chapters, hundreds of words and a lot of grammar: the verb in part 2, the accusative and dative, modals, separable verbs and the Perfekt. Each sentence in the table comes from one chapter. Read them aloud and see how many you can say without looking. The next step is A2, where you will tell longer stories and use new tenses. You are ready for it.

reading.title: Ein Wochenende an der Ostsee
reading.text: Mira, Ben und Leon fahren am Wochenende an die Ostsee. Mira hat einen Plan. Sie sagt: Am Strand kann man faulenzen, und im Wald kann man wandern. Ben nimmt einen Rucksack mit, denn er möchte wandern. Mira nimmt eine Sonnenbrille mit, denn es ist heiß. Leon nimmt ein Zelt mit, denn er möchte campen. Aber im Wald darf man nicht campen. Leon fragt Frau Weber. Sie sagt: Am See darf man campen. Das ist ein guter Vorschlag! Am Abend besichtigen die Freunde eine Burg. Wer macht die Führung? Ein Student macht die Führung. Mit wem wandert Ben am Sonntag? Er wandert mit Leon. Mira faulenzt am Strand.

listening.script:
Leon: Guten Tag. Was kann man hier machen?

reading.title: Mein Wochenende an der Nordsee
reading.text:
Liebe Mira,
viele Grüße von der Nordsee! Ich bin am Freitag mit dem Zug von Hamburg nach Husum gefahren. Die Fahrt hat zwei Stunden gedauert. Husum liegt im Norden an der Küste. Ich übernachte in einer Jugendherberge. Sie ist am Meer, und das Frühstück ist gut. Seit zwei Tagen scheint die Sonne, und es sind 18 Grad. Aber ab Montag regnet es. Am Samstag habe ich die Altstadt besichtigt. Am Sonntag habe ich am Strand gelesen und ein Souvenir für dich gekauft. Das Wochenende war toll, ich habe viel erlebt.
Dein Ben

listening.title: Mira plans the trip to Munich
listening.script:
Leon: Hallo Mira! Was machst du am Wochenende?
Mira: Hallo Leon! Ich fahre nach München. Ich treffe Anna dort.
Leon: Toll! Wann fährt der Zug?
Mira: Um 9 Uhr, auf Gleis 5.
Leon: Wie lange dauert die Fahrt?
Mira: Sechs Stunden. Ich muss in Hannover umsteigen. Zuerst fahre ich von Hamburg nach Hannover. Dann steige ich um. Danach fahre ich nach München.
Leon: Wann kommst du an?
Mira: Um 15 Uhr. Wie ist das Wetter in München?
Leon: München liegt im Süden. Es sind 25 Grad, und die Sonne scheint. Aber ab Donnerstag regnet es.
Mira: Ach so! Dann muss ich einen Regenschirm mitnehmen.
Leon: Ja, genau. Viel Spaß!
